title: Emergencies & Health
description: The phrases to have ready if something goes wrong: calling for help, the police or an ambulance, being ill or hurt, and losing your passport or wallet. The emergency number is 112 in many areas; the police are 110, and an ambulance 118 or 119.

phrases.registerNotes: Shouted, it means Help. Said calmly, tolong starts a polite request: Tolong bantu saya (Please help me).
The police number is 110. A police station is a kantor polisi.
The ambulance numbers are 118 and 119, or 112 for any emergency in many areas.
Ada (there is) works for any emergency: Ada kebakaran! (There's a fire!)
For something milder: Saya kurang enak badan (I'm not feeling very well). Sakit also means sore: sakit kepala is a headache, sakit perut a stomach ache.
Rumah sakit (literally sick house) is a hospital. A klinik is a smaller clinic, and an apotek a pharmacy.
Perlu (need) is plain and polite; butuh means the same.
Point to the spot. Or name it: kepala saya sakit (my head hurts), kaki saya sakit (my leg hurts).
Swap in what you react to: alergi udang (prawns), alergi telur (eggs). For a serious allergy, have it written on your phone too.
phrases.pitfallNote: Kacang covers peanuts, beans and most nuts, and peanuts are everywhere: in satay sauce (bumbu kacang) and gado-gado, for a start.

phrases.registerNotes: Report it at a police station for a written report of the loss (surat kehilangan), which your embassy will want to see. New Zealand's embassy is in Jakarta.
Dicopet is picked from your pocket or bag; dicuri is stolen in general: HP saya dicuri (my phone's been stolen).
Bisa (can) is the everyday way to say you speak a language: Saya bisa sedikit bahasa Indonesia (I speak a little Indonesian).
